entry: American online art community. Launched on August 7, 2000, by Matthew Stephens, Scott Jarkoff and Angelo Sotira, it features artwork, videography, photography and literature. It is headquartered in the Hollywood area of [[Los Angeles]], [[California]]. Wix.com acquired the site in February 2017 for $36 million. Since 2020 many users have left after decisions on site design, AI and NFTs and a large number of scam accounts. The site reached 110 million registered users in 2025.

Mythical personification of evil in many cultures and religious traditions. It is seen as the objectification of a hostile and destructive force. In [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]], the devil is often a tempter who leads people into [[Sin|sin]] and commands [[Demon|demons]]. Names include [[Satan]] in [[Judaism]] and [[Lucifer]] in Christianity, as well as Beelzebub, Mephistopheles, Iblis and Azazil. Jeffrey Burton Russell states that conceptions of the devil can be summed up as a principle of evil independent from God, an aspect of God, a created being turning evil (a fallen angel), or a symbol of human evil. In the Old Testament, evil is an expression of [[Yahweh]]'s wrath. The English word derives from Middle English devel and Old English dēofol, from Latin diabolus, borrowed from Greek diábolos, meaning "slanderer."

Laccolithic butte of igneous rock in northeastern [[Wyoming]]. It rises 1,267 feet (386 m) above the Belle Fourche River, and its summit is 5,112 ft (1,558 m) above sea level. Devils Tower National Monument, established on September 24, 1906, by President [[Theodore Roosevelt]], was the first United States national monument. Magma intruded existing [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary]] layers during the Paleocene Epoch, 56 to 66 million years ago. A 2014 proposal to rename it Bear Lodge was opposed by local state senator Ogden Driskill, and the name was not changed.

Ceremonial county in South West England (pop., 2024: 1,254,506), bordered by the [[English Channel]] to the south and [[Cornwall]] to the west. Its area is 2,590 sq mi (6,700 sq km), and Plymouth is the largest settlement. Dartmoor and Exmoor, two upland moors, have been designated national parks. Part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site lies along the southeast coast. The county gives its name to the [[Devonian]] geologic period.

Fourth period of the [[Paleozoic]] era, spanning 60.7 million years, from 419.62 to 358.86 million years ago. It is named after [[Devon]], South West England, where its rocks were first studied. Free-sporing land plants spread across dry land and formed extensive coal forests, and the first seed-bearing plants appeared by the end of the period. Jawed [[Fish|fish]] diversified so greatly that the period is called the Age of Fishes. The Late Devonian [[Extinction event|extinction]] killed most reef systems, most jawless fishes, placoderms and nearly all [[Trilobite|trilobites]].

Droplets of water that form on exposed objects in the morning or evening. As an exposed surface cools by radiating its heat, atmospheric moisture condenses faster than it can evaporate, forming droplets through [[Condensation|condensation]]. Dew forms most easily on surfaces not warmed by heat from deep ground, such as grass, leaves, railings and car roofs. Cooling is strongest on clear nights, when a surface loses more energy by [[Infrared|infrared]] radiation than it receives from the [[Sun]]. Calm nights favor dew, because wind carries warmer air to cold surfaces. Dew is related to the [[Dew point|dew point]], and when temperatures are low enough it freezes into [[Frost|frost]]. Measured dew rarely exceeds 0.5 mm per night. In regions with long dry seasons, plants such as lichen and pine seedlings benefit from it.

Temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure and absolute humidity, for relative humidity to reach 100%. Below this temperature, [[Water vapor|water vapor]] condenses, forming [[Dew|dew]] on surfaces or [[Fog|fog]] and [[Cloud|clouds]] in the air. Higher moisture content raises the dew point. Below the freezing point of water, the dew point is called the frost point. At a dew point of 20 °C (68 °F), almost everyone feels "sticky."

Proprietary [[Library|library]] classification system that organizes books by discipline and subject. Melvil Dewey first published it in the United States in 1876. It has been revised through 23 major editions, the latest printed in 2011, and is maintained by OCLC, a non-profit cooperative. Each main class is a three-digit number, with decimal extensions for finer subjects. As of 2009 it was used in 200,000 libraries in at least 135 countries. Critics argue that it gives disproportionate space to European history and Protestant [[Christianity]].

American crime television series (2006–2013). Michael C. Hall plays Dexter Morgan, a forensic bloodstain analyst for the Miami Metro Police Department who is also a vigilante [[Serial killer|serial killer]], hunting criminals the justice system failed to punish. The first season adapted Jeff Lindsay's novel *Darkly Dreaming Dexter* (2004). The series finale drew 2.8 million viewers, a record for an original series finale on Showtime at the time. Sequels and a prequel followed.

Capital and largest city of [[Bangladesh]], on the Ganges Delta, with an estimated population of 36.6 million. Dhaka is the second largest city in the world by population and is widely considered the most densely populated built-up urban area. It was the capital of Mughal Bengal for 75 years (1608–39 and 1660–1704) and a hub of the muslin trade in the [[Mughal Empire|Mughal]] period. Under [[British Raj|British rule]] it gained electricity, railways and a modern water supply. It became the capital of an independent Bangladesh in 1971. The city accounts for 35% of Bangladesh's economy, and the Dhaka Stock Exchange has over 750 listed companies. Its Jamdani sari, rickshaw art and Bengali New Year parade have been recognized by [[UNESCO]] as intangible cultural heritage.

Collection of sayings of [[The Buddha|the Buddha]] in verse, one of the most widely read and best known Buddhist scriptures. The original version is in the Khuddaka Nikāya of the Pāli Canon of [[Theravada|Theravāda]] Buddhism. Its title combines [[Dharma|dhamma]], meaning teaching or doctrine, and pada, meaning path or verse. According to tradition, each saying was spoken on a separate occasion, and a 4th or 5th century commentary attributed to Buddhaghosa links the verses to 305 stories. The Pāli text has 423 verses in 26 chapters. Versions in [[Sanskrit]], Gāndhārī and Tibetan, and several Chinese translations, also survive. Brough (2001) found that the Pāli, Gāndhārī and Udānavarga texts have 330 to 340 verses in common.

Key concept in Indian-origin religions, with multiple meanings. From the [[Sanskrit]] root dhr-, meaning to hold or to support, it denotes the law that sustains things, from one's life to society and the universe. In [[Hinduism]], it covers duties, laws and conduct in accord with ṛta, the order that makes life and the universe possible. In [[Buddhism]], it refers to the teachings of [[The Buddha|the Buddha]] and to the true nature of reality. In [[Jainism]], it refers to the teachings of the Tirthankara. In [[Sikhism]], it indicates the path of righteousness. In the 3rd century BCE, the Mauryan emperor [[Ashoka]] translated the word into Greek and Aramaic.

[[India|Indian]] businessman and founder of Reliance Industries. Born in Chorwad, [[Gujarat]], he worked in the yarn trade and founded Reliance in 1958. He took the company public in 1977 and built it into a major conglomerate. He faced accusations of market manipulation, tax evasion and cronyism. In 2016 he was posthumously awarded the Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian honor, for his contributions to trade and industry.

Canid of South, East and Southeast Asia, *Cuon alpinus*, the sole member of its genus. Dholes live in clans of about 12, though groups of over 40 are known, and hunt in packs by day, preferring large and medium-sized [[Ungulate|ungulates]]. In tropical forests they compete with the [[Tiger|tiger]] and leopard, with substantial dietary overlap. The species is now extinct in Central Asia and parts of Southeast Asia. It is listed as Endangered on the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, with fewer than 2,500 mature individuals, because of habitat loss, prey loss, persecution over livestock predation and disease from domestic dogs.

Indian [[Field hockey|field hockey]] player, widely regarded as the greatest in the sport's history. Born in Allahabad (now [[Prayagraj]]), he won three [[Olympic Games|Olympic]] gold medals with India in 1928, 1932 and 1936. Known as the Wizard of hockey for his ball control, he scored 570 goals in 185 matches, according to his autobiography, *Goal*, and over 1,000 goals in his entire career. The BBC called him the "hockey's equivalent of [[Muhammad Ali]]." The Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan in 1956. His birthday, 29 August, is National Sports Day in India.

Variety of a [[Language|language]] spoken by a particular group of people. Dialects differ mainly in [[Phonology|phonology]], [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]], [[Syntax|syntax]] and [[Vocabulary|vocabulary]]. The term most often denotes regional varieties, while varieties defined by [[Social class|social class]] are called sociolects and those of ethnic groups are ethnolects. An idiolect is the speech of one individual. A standard dialect is supported by institutions such as government recognition, schooling, dictionaries and grammars; the [[French language|French]] language, for example, is supported by the Académie Française. Nonstandard dialects have complete grammars but little institutional support. The line between dialect and language is often arbitrary and based on social, political or historical considerations.

Method of philosophical argument that advances thought by resolving contradictions. The term comes from [[Ancient Greek]] *dialegesthai*, meaning "to converse," and was popularized by [[Plato]]'s Socratic dialogues, in which people with different views sought truth through reasoned argument. [[Aristotle]] redefined it as a method for examining reputable opinions. [[Immanuel Kant]] described a "logic of illusion" arising from [[Contradiction|contradictions]] that reason meets beyond experience. [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel|Hegel]] regarded contradiction as the driving force of all development. [[Karl Marx]] reconfigured the method on a materialist basis, arguing that history is driven by class struggle. [[Theodor W. Adorno]] later developed a "negative dialectics."

Mineral form of [[Carbon|carbon]], with its atoms arranged in a cubic crystal structure. It is the hardest and most thermally conductive natural material, which makes it useful for [[Abrasive|cutting]] and polishing tools. Its rigid lattice admits few impurities, but about one per million lattice atoms can color it blue (boron), yellow (nitrogen), brown or green. Most natural diamonds are between 1 billion and 3.5 billion years old and formed 150 to 250 km deep in the Earth's mantle. Volcanic eruptions carried them to the surface in [[Igneous rock|igneous]] kimberlites and lamproites. In 1772 [[Antoine Lavoisier]] showed that burning diamond in oxygen produced only [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], proving it is carbon. [[Graphite|Graphite]] is the stable form of carbon at room temperature and pressure.

[[Mahayana|Mahāyāna]] [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] sutra of the Prajñāpāramitā ("perfection of wisdom") genre. Its title, *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, uses the *vajra*, a diamond or thunderbolt, as a metaphor for wisdom that cuts illusions. It is one of the most influential Mahayana sutras in East Asia, especially in the [[Zen]] tradition. The first Chinese translation is thought to have been made around 401 by [[Kumārajīva]], whose version is the most widely used. A copy from the [[Tang dynasty]] was discovered among the Dunhuang manuscripts in 1900. Dated May 11, 868, it is broadly considered the oldest extant printed book. Its colophon states it was made "for universal free distribution," an early [[Public domain|public domain]] dedication.

British royal, first wife of [[Charles III]] and mother of Princes William and Harry. She married Charles, then Prince of Wales, in 1981 and became Princess of Wales. The couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. She represented [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] at functions across the Commonwealth realms and became known for her work on AIDS and the international removal of landmines. Her death in a car crash in Paris led to extensive public mourning. An inquest returned a verdict of unlawful killing due to gross negligence by a driver and by the paparazzi pursuing her.

American singer and actress, lead singer of [[The Supremes|the Supremes]]. The group became [[Motown]]'s most successful act of the 1960s. As a solo artist from 1970, she had six Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles, including "Touch Me in the Morning" and "Endless Love." Her portrayal of [[Billie Holiday]] in *Lady Sings the Blues* (1972) earned her a Golden Globe Award and an Academy Award nomination. She has sold over 100 million records as a solo artist. She was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1988 as a member of the Supremes.

American actress associated with the [[New Hollywood]] movement. She appeared in eight films by [[Woody Allen]] and won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Annie Hall* (1977). Her other roles include Kay Adams in *The Godfather* (1972) and its sequels, and Louise Bryant in *Reds* (1981). She was also Oscar-nominated for *Marvin's Room* (1996) and *Something's Gotta Give* (2003). Keaton directed three films and a documentary and wrote four books, including the memoir *Then Again* (2011).

American television journalist and news anchor. She was a staff assistant in the White House of [[Richard Nixon]] and helped with his post-presidency memoirs. At CBS News she became the first woman correspondent on *60 Minutes* and hosted *CBS Morning*. At ABC News she anchored *World News Tonight*, *Good Morning America* and *20/20*. Her documentaries and interview specials have earned multiple Emmy Awards.

American actress and two-time winner of the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Supporting Actress. Both Oscars were for films directed by [[Woody Allen]]: *Hannah and Her Sisters* (1986) and *Bullets Over Broadway* (1994). She also won a Golden Globe for *Bullets Over Broadway* and the 2008 Primetime Emmy Award for her role in *In Treatment*. Early in her career she spent four years as a member of the Arena Stage in [[Washington, D.C.]] Her other films include *Edward Scissorhands* (1990) and *The Birdcage* (1996).

Undergarment that absorbs or contains urine and feces, worn mainly by [[Infant|infants]]. In Britain and Australia it is called a nappy. Diapers are made of cloth such as [[Cotton|cotton]], [[Hemp|hemp]] or [[Bamboo|bamboo]], or of disposable materials containing absorbent chemicals. Toddlers not yet toilet trained, children who wet the bed, and adults with incontinence or [[Disability|disability]] also use them, as do [[Astronaut|astronauts]] in extreme conditions. Failure to change a diaper regularly can cause skin problems. Cloth diapers were first mass-produced in the [[United States]] in 1887 by Maria Allen.
